chunks: Ahmad ibn Harun al-Fami, may God have mercy on him, narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Ja'far al-Himyari narrated to us from his father. He said: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr narrated to us from Hisham ibn Salim from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad, peace be upon him. He said:
Poverty nearly becomes disbelief, and envy nearly overcomes destiny.

key_terms.الْحَسَدُ: Envy; wishing that another's blessings be removed
key_terms.الْفَقْرُ: Poverty; material deprivation that threatens spiritual wellbeing
key_terms.الْقَدَرَ: Destiny; God's predetermined decree and apportionment
key_terms.كُفْرًا: Disbelief; denial or ingratitude toward God

ai.seo_question: Why does Imam al-Sadiq say poverty nearly becomes disbelief and envy nearly overcomes destiny?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Amali of Shaykh al-Saduq, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) delivers a profound aphorism about two dangerous human conditions. Poverty is so spiritually perilous that it can drive a person to the brink of disbelief, as deprivation may lead one to question God's wisdom and justice. Envy is so destructive that it nearly overcomes divine destiny itself, because the envious person effectively rejects God's distribution of blessings. This teaching was directed at the early Muslim community to warn against both the spiritual dangers of material deprivation and the moral corruption of jealousy.
word_analysis: may God have mercy on him

en.bilal-muhammad: Ahmad b. Harun al-Fami (rh) narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. `Abdullah b. Ja`far al-Himyari narrated to us from his father. He said: Muhammad b. `Abd al-Jabbar narrated to us. He said: Muhammad b. Abi `Umayr narrated to us from Hisham b. Salim from al-Sadiq Ja`far b. Muhammad (as). He said:
Poverty can incline into disbelief, and envy can incline into the changing of destiny.
